children: Bitcoin and gold both took a hit in the latest market sell-off. According to Fidelity's Jurrien Timmer, only one of them handled it with any grace.
Timmer, Fidelity's Director of Global Macro, says he prefers Bitcoin over gold right now. His reasoning is simple: Bitcoin's price measured against gold has held up while both assets slid.
Timmer isn't saying Bitcoin went up while gold went down. Both assets declined during the sell-off, which the research places around November 6-7.
His focus is the ratio between them. On that scoreboard, Bitcoin looks strong. One Bitcoin bought approximately 12 ounces of gold at its low point in this cycle. It now buys roughly 21 ounces.
The move has also pushed Bitcoin above the recent trading range it held against gold. For technical analysts, a break like that often signals a change in leadership between two assets.
Timmer has a habit of tracking these shifts closely. He has recorded several rotations of speculative capital between Bitcoin and gold since late 2025.
Those rotations picked up after Bitcoin peaked close to $126,000 in 2025 and gold's own momentum began to fade.
Timmer's preference lines up with where institutional money has been going. Since 2024, spot Bitcoin ETFs have pulled in nearly $55 billion in inflows.
Gold and silver exchange-traded products, by comparison, have attracted around $29 billion over the same stretch. That puts Bitcoin funds at roughly double the precious metals haul.
Both Bitcoin and gold have recently shown a correlation of 60-70% with the S&P 500. In other words, when stocks fall, these two have tended to fall alongside them.
Timmer has not abandoned gold entirely. He continues to endorse both assets as tools for diversifying against monetary and fiscal instability.
His current lean toward Bitcoin is about near-term prospects. It is a tactical tilt, not a declaration that gold has lost its place in a portfolio.
For investors, the Bitcoin-to-gold ratio is a useful lens because it strips out the noise of the dollar. It shows how two competing hedges stack up against each other directly.

The recovery from about 12 ounces to about 21 ounces suggests the pendulum has swung back toward Bitcoin, at least for now. Timmer's own record of documented rotations, however, is a reminder that this pendulum has swung several times recently.
The most immediate takeaway is that a prominent Fidelity strategist sees Bitcoin holding its ground better than gold under pressure.
The ETF flow data supports the idea that institutions are already leaning this way. A gap of nearly $55 billion versus around $29 billion is hard to dismiss as a rounding error.
Yet the high correlation with stocks is a real risk. If both assets keep tracking the S&P 500 at 60-70%, their value as diversifiers shrinks during broad market drawdowns.
Timmer's position sits somewhere in the middle. He holds both as hedges against monetary and fiscal turbulence while tilting toward the one showing better relative strength.

title: Fidelity's Jurrien Timmer favors Bitcoin over gold amid sell-off
